subject: Geography
description: Alluvial, black, red, laterite soils and crops

questions.stem: The most widespread soil type in India, found in the northern plains, is:

options.option_text: Black soil
Alluvial soil
Red soil
Laterite soil

questions.explanation: Alluvial soils cover about 40 % of India's land — deposited by the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra river systems and their tributaries. Very fertile; good for wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute. Two types: older Bhangar (on higher ground) and newer Khadar (on flood plains). Black cotton soil (regur) is next; red and laterite soils follow.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Black cotton soil (regur), ideal for cotton cultivation, is formed from the weathering of:

options.option_text: Granite
Basalt lava
Limestone
Sandstone

questions.explanation: Black cotton soil / regur — formed from the weathering of the Deccan Trap basalt lava flows. Found in Maharashtra, western MP, Gujarat, northern Karnataka, Telangana. Rich in calcium, potassium, magnesium; poor in nitrogen and organic matter. Retains moisture well — holds up well through the long dry season, which is why it suits cotton. Granite weathers to red soil.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Red soils of India owe their colour to:

options.option_text: Humus content
Ferric oxide
Calcium carbonate
Potassium salts

questions.explanation: Red soils get their colour from ferric (iron) oxide — formed in conditions of good aeration. They cover ~10 % of India — much of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra, parts of Odisha, Jharkhand, eastern MP. Relatively poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus; respond well to irrigation and fertilisers. Suit millets, groundnut, tobacco. Humus gives soil a dark-brown colour. iron oxide.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Laterite soils of India are formed in areas of:

options.option_text: Cold and dry climate
High temperature and heavy rainfall
Semi-arid plateau climate
Tropical desert climate

questions.explanation: Laterite soils — formed by intense leaching in high temperature + heavy rainfall. Silica is washed out, leaving iron and aluminium oxides. Found on the Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra), Eastern Ghats (Odisha), NE hills, and the Malwa and Chhotanagpur plateaus. Poor in fertility; suited to cashew, tapioca, rubber, coffee, tea (with fertilisation). Laterite bricks are used in construction in Kerala and coastal Karnataka.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Match the soil type with the region where it dominates. A. Alluvial. B. Black (regur). C. Red. D. Laterite. List-II: 1. Indo-Gangetic plain, 2. Deccan plateau (Maharashtra, western MP), 3. Tamil Nadu / Karnataka uplands, 4. Kerala / Western Ghats.
questions.explanation: Alluvial — Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plain. Black (regur) — Deccan trap region of Maharashtra, western MP, Gujarat, northern Karnataka, Telangana. Red — Tamil Nadu, Karnataka uplands, eastern MP, Jharkhand. Laterite — Kerala + high-rainfall Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats highlands. Mountain/forest soils exist in the Himalayan belt; desert (arid) soils in western Rajasthan.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which soil retains moisture for long periods, swells when wet and shrinks (forming cracks) when dry?

options.option_text: Alluvial soil
Black cotton soil (regur)
Red soil
Arid soil

questions.explanation: Black cotton soil is rich in clay (montmorillonite) that absorbs water and swells; on drying, it shrinks and develops deep cracks — 'self-ploughing' nature. This helps it retain moisture and suits rain-fed cotton over long dry seasons. Alluvial soils drain more freely; red soils are coarser; arid soils are sandy with little clay.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Arid (desert) soils of Rajasthan are deficient in:

options.option_text: Calcium and iron
Nitrogen and humus
Potassium and phosphate
Sodium and potassium

questions.explanation: Arid / desert soils are sandy (60-90 % sand), poor in nitrogen and humus (low organic matter because of sparse vegetation), but relatively rich in calcium and phosphates. They develop a calcareous kankar-hard pan below the surface. Can support crops like bajra, jowar, pulses where irrigated via canals like the Indira Gandhi Canal.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Khadar and Bhangar are two sub-types of which major soil group in India?

options.option_text: Alluvial soil deposited by Himalayan river systems
Black cotton soil formed from Deccan trap basalt
Laterite soil leached by heavy monsoon rainfall
Red soil derived from crystalline igneous rocks

questions.explanation: Alluvial soil is subdivided into Khadar (newer, lighter, found near active floodplains, more fertile) and Bhangar (older, darker, on higher terraces, contains kankar nodules). Black, laterite, and red soils have no such sub-classification by age/position of deposition.

questions.stem: Salt-affected soils in the Indo-Gangetic plains that render land unfit for cultivation are locally known as:

options.option_text: Khadar — younger alluvial soil close to active riverbeds
Bhangar — older alluvial soil on higher inland terraces
Usar or Reh — saline and alkaline barren soil tracts
Terai — marshy waterlogged forested lowland zone

questions.explanation: Usar (also Reh or Kallar) refers to saline-alkaline soils in UP, Haryana, and Punjab where capillary action deposits sodium salts at the surface, making land infertile. Khadar and Bhangar are sub-types of alluvial soil distinguished by age, not salinity. Terai is a geographical zone, not a soil type.

questions.stem: Though black (regur) soil is self-ploughing and rich in calcium and iron, it typically requires fertiliser inputs because it is deficient in which pair of plant nutrients?

options.option_text: Nitrogen and phosphorus — the primary growth-limiting nutrients
Calcium and potassium — essential for cell wall and enzyme work
Iron and manganese — trace elements needed for chlorophyll
Magnesium and sulphur — secondary macronutrients for seed oil

questions.explanation: Black soil is notably deficient in nitrogen and phosphorus, which limits crop productivity despite being naturally rich in calcium, magnesium, iron, and potassium. Calcium and potassium are present in abundance (not deficient), making option B a classic distractor — students assume richness in one pair implies deficiency in the other.

questions.stem: Peaty and marshy soils, characterised by very high organic matter and humus content, are predominantly found in which of the following regions of India?

options.option_text: Arid zones of western Rajasthan and the Rann of Kutch
Rain-shadow interior of the Deccan plateau in Karnataka
Kerala backwaters, Sundarbans delta, and Odisha coast
High-altitude cold deserts of Ladakh and Spiti valley

questions.explanation: Peaty/marshy soils form in waterlogged, high-rainfall or coastal low-lying areas where organic matter accumulates faster than it decomposes. The Kerala backwaters (kuttanad), Sundarbans mangrove delta, and Odisha coast are the classic Indian examples. Rajasthan and Ladakh have arid/cold desert soils; the Deccan interior is the domain of black soil.

questions.stem: Cashew nut cultivation in India is concentrated in Goa, Kerala, and coastal Karnataka primarily because the crop thrives in which soil type found abundantly in these areas?

options.option_text: Alluvial soil along river plains of peninsular coastal belts
Black cotton soil of the Maharashtra and Karnataka plateau
Laterite soil — well-drained, acidic, and iron-oxide rich
Mountain forest soil of the northeastern Himalayan foothills

questions.explanation: Cashew nut thrives in laterite soils because the crop tolerates poor, well-drained, acidic soil conditions and does not need high fertility — exactly the profile of laterite. Black cotton soil retains too much moisture and cracks when dry, unsuitable for cashew roots. Alluvial soil is fertile but often waterlogged in coastal zones.

questions.stem: During laterisation under tropical wet-dry climates, the key geochemical process that distinguishes laterite from other soils is:

options.option_text: Silica and soluble bases leach out while iron and aluminium oxides accumulate
Iron and aluminium wash downward while silica concentrates at the surface layer
Humus builds up rapidly due to inhibited bacterial decomposition in warmth
Capillary rise brings carbonates and salts upward, cementing a surface hardpan

questions.explanation: Laterisation is the intense leaching of silica (desilication) and soluble bases (Ca, Mg, K) under alternating wet-dry tropical conditions, leaving behind a residual accumulation of sesquioxides of iron (Fe₂O₃ — giving the brick-red colour) and aluminium (Al₂O₃). Option B reverses the direction of movement — the classic examiner trap. Capillary salt concentration (option D) describes saline soil formation, not laterite.

questions.stem: In the USDA Soil Taxonomy — the international classification system referenced in Indian soil science literature — black cotton soil (Regur) of the Deccan plateau is classified under which soil order?

options.option_text: Alfisols — moderately leached soils with subsurface clay accumulation
Vertisols — shrink-swell clay soils rich in montmorillonite mineral
Ultisols — highly weathered acidic soils with low base saturation
Inceptisols — young soils with only weakly developed horizon profiles

questions.explanation: Vertisols are defined by their high content of expansive 2:1 montmorillonite clay, which swells markedly when wet and shrinks and cracks on drying — the defining behaviour of Regur/black cotton soil. Alfisols (option A) is a common distractor because laterite-adjacent soils in humid tropics fall there; Ultisols are the highly weathered red-yellow soils; Inceptisols are young soils, the opposite of the mature, deep Regur profile.
